title: The Gosinga grove
hook: which monk would light up the grove? each answers from his own practice

segments.voice: Yesterday: samagga, three friends who didn't keep score. Did you fill one empty jar for someone, quietly? Today we go back to the same wood, on a different night. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

It's a clear night with the moon full. The sal trees are in bloom, and the text says the whole wood smells as if heavenly scents were drifting through it. Six of the Buddha's great disciples have gathered in the Gosinga grove. Sariputta looks around and asks the others a question that sounds almost like a parlor game: what kind of monk would light up this grove? Everyone answers. Nobody gives the same answer. Today: the Gosinga grove.
screen: `A FULL MOON, THE SAL TREES IN BLOOM.` → `SIX GREAT DISCIPLES.` → `WHO WOULD LIGHT UP THIS GROVE?`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-second discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the greater discourse in Gosinga. Listen to the answers. Ananda, who memorized the teachings, says: a monk who has learned much and remembers it, and teaches it clearly. Revata says: a monk who delights in solitary meditation. Anuruddha, known for his inner sight, says: a monk who sees a thousand worlds with the divine eye. Mahakassapa, the strict forest monk, says: one who lives in the forest, eats only alms food, wears rag robes, wants little, and praises those things to others. Moggallana says: two monks discussing the teaching deeply, asking and answering without faltering. And Sariputta says: a monk who masters his own mind, who can rest in whatever state he chooses in the morning, at noon or at evening, like a king with a chest full of clothes who wears whatever color he likes. Do you hear it? Each one names his own practice. That's not vanity. It's honesty. You can only praise what you actually love. Then they go to the Buddha and ask: who spoke best? And he says: all of you spoke well, each in your own way. Then he gives his own answer: a monk who sits down after his meal, legs crossed, body straight, determined not to get up until his mind is free. The Buddha doesn't rank them. A community is lit by many lamps, and the light is different from each one. The learner, the hermit, the seer, the ascetic, the debater, the master of mind. One grove.
screen: `SIX ANSWERS UNDER A FULL MOON` · `EACH NAMES THE PRACTICE HE LOVES` · `ALL OF YOU SPOKE WELL` · `THE BUDDHA: SIT UNTIL THE MIND IS FREE` · then, large: `EACH LIGHTS IT DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what lights your grove. Sit, and ask yourself Sariputta's question. Not what should light it, but what actually does, for you. Is it learning something and understanding it? Quiet time alone? Wanting less? A good conversation? Steadying your mind? Let one answer come. Don't argue with it. Then sit for the rest of the time the way the Buddha described: body straight, settled, simply here. The bell holds the time.
Gosinga. A wood of blooming sal trees, a full moon, and six disciples who each light it in their own way. Today's word.
Your line: each lights it differently. Today, notice one person whose way of practicing or working isn't yours, and name to yourself the light they bring. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist traditions honor many temperaments of practice, from study and teaching to forest asceticism and meditation, and MN 32 is often taught as a picture of a community where each kind of practitioner has a place.

fork.setup: six disciples come to you, each with a different answer to the question 'who would light up this grove?' they ask which one is best. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
options: all of you spoke well, each in your own way.
none of you; only I light the grove.
fork.reveal: the Buddha affirms every answer, and then adds his own: a monk who sits determined not to rise until his mind is free.

original.note: Pali gosinga: cow's horn (go, cow + singa, horn), the name of the sal-tree wood.

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one right way to be a good practitioner.
what it means: a community is lit by many kinds of practice, each honest about what it loves.
what a scholar hears: MN 32's answers match each disciple's title elsewhere in the canon, such as Anuruddha foremost in the divine eye and Mahakassapa in ascetic practices (AN 1).

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 32, Mahagosinga Sutta (the greater discourse in Gosinga)
